chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar (may God be pleased with him) narrated from his father, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Sayyari, from Ali ibn Asbat, who linked it up to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), saying:
Whoever is not angered by slight neglect (or rudeness) will not be grateful for blessings.

key_terms.جَفْوَة: Slight neglect, rudeness, or minor offense that might provoke anger

ai.seo_question: What is the connection between patience with slights and gratitude for blessings in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In al-Khisal, Shaykh al-Saduq presents this hadith to illustrate that true gratitude (shukr) is not merely verbal acknowledgment but a deep spiritual state rooted in emotional stability. Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) teaches that the capacity to overlook minor slights (jafwah) without anger reflects a heart purified from ego, which is the prerequisite for recognizing and thanking God for His continuous favors. This links the ethical virtue of forbearance directly to the theological concept of thankfulness, suggesting that one who cannot endure slight offense lacks the humility required for genuine worship.

en.dr-ali-peiravi: 1-38 Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar - may God be pleased with him - narrated that his father quoted on the authority of Muhammad ibn Ahmad, on the authority of Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Sayyari, on the authority of Ali ibn Asbat who linked it up to Aba Abdullah as-Sadiq (MGB) saying,
“Whoever is not angered when oppressed would not thank for blessings.”
